meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 9: restructuring and turnaround, the firms that are called when the money runs out
meldungen.text:
Most strategy consultants are hired to help a healthy company grow. Restructuring consultants are hired when a company may not survive the next quarter: covenants are about to be breached, liquidity is draining, lenders are losing patience, or a formal insolvency procedure (Chapter 11 in the United States, a protective shield or StaRUG process in Germany) is already under way. The work is fast, numerical and uncomfortably close to real consequences: thirteen-week cash flow forecasts, liquidity management, cost cutting, negotiations between the company, its banks and its bondholders, and sometimes running the business itself.

Career guides consistently name three firms as the top tier: Alvarez and Marsal (A&M), AlixPartners and FTI Consulting. What sets them apart, according to Management Consulted and Hacking the Case Interview, is a combination that classic strategy houses lack: credibility in court, the ability to install their own people as interim executives (chief restructuring officer, interim CFO), and enough scale to staff a global Chapter 11 case within a week. Size estimates vary widely by source. Revelio Labs counts roughly 15,800 employees at A&M and about 4,500 at AlixPartners; FTI, the only one of the three that is listed and publishes accounts, reported revenue of about 3.8 billion dollars for 2025, of which its corporate finance and restructuring segment contributed roughly two fifths. AlixPartners strengthened its automotive and DACH presence in 2024 by acquiring Berylls, a Munich-based specialist, which brought around 160 professionals in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and beyond. In the German-speaking market, Roland Berger's restructuring practice, which part 5 of this series covered, is the strategy firm that competes most directly.

How the career works: you typically join as an analyst or associate, and the learning curve is steep and financial. You build cash models, sit in on lender meetings and, at A&M in particular, may be embedded in the client's finance department for months. The culture is more operational and less slide-driven than at MBB, the hours are heavy during live cases, and the work is countercyclical: when the economy weakens and defaults rise, restructuring teams get busier.

The exits follow from the skill set. Guides and practitioners point most often to distressed credit funds and hedge funds, special situations private equity, restructuring or M&A advisory at investment banks, and turnaround or interim management roles inside companies. AlixPartners alumni, according to one guide, also move into venture capital, private equity, financial services and start-ups, and many complete an MBA. A&M is described as excellent preparation for finance and advisory careers, but less so for unrelated industries. The longer-term paths are CFO, chief restructuring officer or partner in a turnaround practice. An honest caveat: there is no firm-published data on where analysts actually land, so these patterns rest on career guides and practitioner forums rather than statistics.

For a candidate coming out of a European Master in Management, the trade-off is clear. Restructuring gives you financial depth and credibility with investors faster than generalist strategy work, but it narrows your profile towards finance. If you are drawn to private equity or credit investing and like hard numbers more than broad strategy questions, it is a serious alternative to Tier 2 strategy firms; if you want maximum optionality, MBB or a strong strategy boutique keeps more doors open.

meldungen.titel: Claude Ship: Anthropic lets Claude review, fix and now approve code on its own
meldungen.text:
Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a product that moves pull requests (the proposed changes to a codebase) automatically through review, repair and approval. "The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it," the company wrote. It is available in beta for Claude Team and Enterprise customers whose code lives on GitHub.

Claude Ship has three parts. Code Review, announced in March and generally available since October, checks a pull request against the entire codebase, verifies its own findings and posts them directly to the request. Two agents are new. PR Steward steps in when automated checks fail, when branches conflict or when reviewers leave feedback; it fixes the problem, explains what it changed and how to undo it, but may not approve or merge anything. That is the job of Claude Approvals, which approves routine changes if an organisation's policy allows it. Teams write that policy as a file in the repository, which Anthropic likens to "a smarter CODEOWNERS file", and can require human sign-off for sensitive cases; Anthropic recommends starting in observe-only mode. Individual developers can use the same pipeline through a new /ship command in Claude Code.

Anthropic backs the launch with its own numbers: on the Claude Code team, merged pull requests more than doubled between June and September, while the share of changes that later had to be reverted fell by more than 40 per cent. Usage is billed by tokens with admin spending limits, and eligible Enterprise customers can claim at least 10,000 dollars in credits. Organisations using zero data retention, the HIPAA configuration or customer-managed encryption keys are excluded for now.

Strategically, the move mirrors what Anthropic did with Cowork, which it folded into the main app with Claude Docs, Slides, Sheets and Whiteboards: deepen an existing product so that users stay on the platform. Claude Code is Anthropic's largest source of revenue, and the company argues that once agents write most of the code, the bottleneck shifts to everything after the pull request. It competes there with GitHub Copilot's reviews, CodeRabbit and Cursor's Bugbot. It is also Anthropic's first major launch since its stock market debut last Thursday, and the market was unmoved: the shares closed at 87.64 dollars on Monday, down 1.4 per cent on the day and more than 21 per cent below the first trade of 111.50 dollars, though still about 6 per cent above the IPO price of 83 dollars.

meldungen.titel: Harvard Business School's MBA applications fall 18 per cent, and it deliberately shrinks its class
meldungen.text:
Harvard Business School received 7,682 applications for its MBA Class of 2028, 18.4 per cent fewer than a year earlier, Poets and Quants reports. Rather than dig deeper into its pool, HBS chose to cut its entering class to 906 students. For context, the previous class drew 9,409 applications and enrolled 943, according to the GMAC class profile, and the Class of 2026 had attracted 9,856 applicants. Harvard's pool has thus shrunk by roughly a fifth in two years.

The decline fits a wider pattern that Poets and Quants describes as an inflection point for the MBA: applications to American programmes are falling sharply, raising questions about the future of the two-year degree. A smaller class lets Harvard protect its selectivity and the quality of its intake while demand cools.

The employment side looks healthier. In a separate report, Harvard's Class of 2026 had accepted offers from 94 per cent of job seekers, and technology took 25 per cent of accepted offers, its highest share since at least 2014, almost catching financial services at 27 per cent. Finance had led comfortably for more than a decade.

meldungen.titel: Trump says he "made the deal" to reinstate Nvidia's chief, as Washington blacklists the chip buyer at the heart of the scandal
meldungen.text:
Jensen Huang is back in charge of Nvidia less than two weeks after resigning, and the White House openly claims the credit. Huang, who co-founded the AI chipmaker in 1993, stepped down on 12 November after revelations of extramarital affairs, one of them reportedly with Alice Huang (no relation), a former chief executive of the Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom US intelligence suspects of working for Beijing. China denies the spying allegation. Last Tuesday the board said explicitly that it did not intend to bring him back. On Monday it reversed course.

President Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to the board and "made the deal". The directors, he said, asked for assurances on national security, "and we gave them assurances at least with everything we know." Board chairman Harvey Jones said the board had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident the move posed no security risk. Markets cheered: Nvidia's share price jumped 31 per cent, adding almost 1 trillion dollars in market value, although the stock remains below its level of a month ago.

The same day, the Commerce Department announced that it would add Megaspeed and its subsidiary Speedmatrix to the Entity List, which bars companies from trading goods in the United States. The department says it has investigated the firm for almost two years on suspicion of channelling Nvidia's advanced chips to Chinese buyers, which US export controls have prohibited since 2022. No effective date was given.

The political fallout is bipartisan. Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become Speaker when Democrats take the House in January, called the reinstatement "indefensible", and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, called it reckless. Republican Tom Cotton, who chairs the Senate intelligence committee, said the Megaspeed affair was "just the tip of the iceberg". A BBC review of Trump's financial disclosures found Nvidia share purchases worth between 23 and 86 million dollars over two years; the White House rejects any suggestion that he profits from the presidency and says his businesses sit in a trust run by his sons. Democrats eyeing 2028 are already folding the episode into their corruption message.

Next: Huang faces a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December and has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee two days later.

meldungen.titel: Vienna's coalition prepares a 750 million euro electricity subsidy for industry while it consolidates the budget
meldungen.text:
The decision. Austria's governing parties, ÖVP, SPÖ and Neos, want to fix a three-year relief package for industrial electricity costs before the end of December. Up to 750 million euros are earmarked for 2027 to 2029, or 250 million a year, covering a new industrial electricity price and an extended electricity cost compensation scheme (SAG+). According to the Wirtschaftskammer (WKO), from January 2027 eligible energy-intensive companies and their suppliers would pay at most 5 cents per kilowatt hour on half of their consumption. Separately, the electricity levy for companies is to fall to 0.82 cents per kilowatt hour.

The case made. The government and the Industriellenvereinigung argue that high power prices weigh on energy-intensive production in Austria, all the more because Germany is introducing its own subsidised industrial power price. Critics question the timing and the target. Der Standard notes that the coalition has pledged to cut subsidies and consolidate the budget, yet is launching a new one that industry lobbyists and the ÖVP pushed for, and that the SPÖ-led finance ministry raised objections during the parliamentary consultation. The FPÖ, from the other side, calls 10 cents for households "still far too high".

The numbers. The finance ministry expects a general government deficit of 4.1 per cent of GDP for 2026, or 21.4 billion euros, and debt of 440.3 billion euros, 82.4 per cent of GDP (BMF, October 2026). The Fiskalrat estimates that a deficit of around 2.5 per cent of GDP would be needed to stabilise the debt ratio (Fiskalrat, 2026). Against that, 250 million euros a year is about 1.2 per cent of the 2026 deficit: material, but not decisive. The WKO had demanded a 5 cent price for three years at an estimated 400 million euros a year, so the package is smaller than industry wanted. On prices, the EU average for non-household electricity was 0.18 euros per kilowatt hour in the first half of 2026, down 5.4 per cent year on year (Eurostat, November 2026). A study for Oesterreichs Energie found that Austrian industrial prices have been somewhat above the EU average since 2022 but have fallen markedly since 2023.

Reality check. The data support the claim that power costs rose sharply during the energy crisis and that Austria sits above the EU average. They do not show that the gap is still widening: prices are falling across Europe. The competitive argument against Germany is plausible, since Berlin is subsidising its own industry, but no published estimate quantifies how many jobs or how much output the Austrian scheme would protect. Whether a consolidating state should subsidise particular sectors is a value judgement that data cannot settle. What remains unknown is the expected effect per euro spent and which companies will benefit most.

Evidence rating: Partly grounded. The price and budget figures are real and the scheme is modest relative to the deficit, but the core claim that it secures jobs and investment rests on no published impact estimate.
